```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 3.4, fig.align = "center")
library(karma2d)
```

A fitted 2-D KARMA model describes the "normal" spatial behaviour of an
image. Pixels that the model finds hard to explain have large quantile
residuals, so the residuals can be monitored like a Shewhart control chart
(Phase II) after the model has been calibrated on an anomaly-free window
(Phase I). Morphological opening then removes isolated false alarms. This
vignette illustrates the procedure with the NDVI scene `ndvi_paraiba` and an
artificial anomaly. The anomaly is injected by hand, so detection performance
here is a demonstration and not a validation on real events.

## Data and Phase I

`ndvi_paraiba` is a 100 x 100 NDVI image with values in $(-1, 1)$. As in the
article we rescale it to $(0,1)$ with $y = (x + 1)/2$ and use the lower-right
50 x 50 block as the Phase I (calibration) window.

```{r data}
y <- (ndvi_paraiba + 1) / 2
phase1 <- y[51:100, 51:100]
fit <- karma2d_fit(phase1, order = c(1, 0))
summary(fit)
```

Quantile residuals of the calibration window should look roughly standard
normal, which justifies limits such as $\pm 3$. Here the bulk is close to
normal, with a somewhat heavier right tail (about 1% of the pixels exceed 3 in
absolute value):

```{r phase1-resid}
r1 <- karma2d_residuals(fit, newdata = phase1, padding = "duplicate")
hist(r1, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, main = "Phase I quantile residuals",
     xlab = "residual")
curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, lwd = 2)
c(sd = sd(r1), outside_3 = sum(abs(r1) > 3))
```

## Phase II: an injected anomaly

We copy the whole scene and set a 16 x 16 block (rows 5-20, columns 15-30) to
a constant value of 0.3, far below the surrounding vegetation level. The
residuals are computed for the **whole** scene with the Phase I model. The
`padding = "duplicate"` option gives a residual for every pixel, including the
first row and column.

```{r inject}
y_anom <- y
y_anom[5:20, 15:30] <- 0.3
truth <- matrix(FALSE, nrow(y), ncol(y))
truth[5:20, 15:30] <- TRUE

res <- karma2d_residuals(fit, newdata = y_anom, padding = "duplicate")
summary(as.vector(res))
```

## Control limits and morphological post-processing

`karma2d_detect_anomalies()` flags pixels whose residual lies outside
$\pm$`limit` (here 3) and then applies a morphological operation with a
structuring element; the default is opening with a 3 x 3 square, which
removes isolated flagged pixels and small groups smaller than the element.
For elongated features other shapes are possible (the GRDI application in
the article uses a 3 x 5 element), e.g.
`karma2d_structuring_element(3, 5)`.

```{r detect}
det <- karma2d_detect_anomalies(res, limit = 3,
                                structuring_element =
                                  karma2d_structuring_element(3, 3),
                                morphology = "opening")
det
```

```{r maps, fig.height = 3.6}
show <- function(m, main, col = hcl.colors(32, "viridis"), ...) {
  image(t(m[rev(seq_len(nrow(m))), ]), main = main, axes = FALSE,
        col = col, ...)
}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
show(y_anom, "Scene with anomaly")
show(pmax(pmin(res, 6), -6), "Residuals (clipped)",
     col = hcl.colors(32, "Blue-Red 3"), zlim = c(-6, 6))
show(det$threshold_mask * 1, "Outside +/-3", col = c("white", "black"))
show(det$detected_mask * 1, "After opening", col = c("white", "black"))
par(op)
```

Isolated flagged pixels in the threshold mask (second black panel) are natural
false alarms: with a standard normal reference a limit of 3 flags about 0.27%
of the pixels even without anomalies. Opening removes most of them.

## Performance metrics

Because the true anomaly is known we can compute the pixel-wise confusion
counts.

```{r confusion}
tp <- sum(det$detected_mask & truth)
fp <- sum(det$detected_mask & !truth)
fn <- sum(!det$detected_mask & truth)
c(recall = tp / (tp + fn), precision = tp / (tp + fp),
  detected = sum(det$detected_mask), true_anomaly = sum(truth))
```

The whole injected block is recovered (recall 1); the extra detected pixels
are a thin rim along the bottom and right edges of the block (one pixel wide
in this run), where pixels have anomalous pixels as their upper and left
neighbours and therefore are mispredicted too. This is why
precision is below one.

`karma2d_metrics()` computes MAE, MSE, SMAPE (in percent) and RMSLE of the
predicted median against the observed image. We evaluate the clean scene on
the calibration region and on the full scene (all on the rescaled $(0,1)$
scale):

```{r metrics}
pred <- predict(fit, newdata = y, padding = "duplicate")
calib <- karma2d_metrics(y[51:100, 51:100], pred[51:100, 51:100])
full  <- karma2d_metrics(y, pred)
rbind(calibration = calib, full_scene = full)
```

Accuracy on the full scene is similar to (here slightly better than) that on
the calibration window; the model was fitted only to the latter, so this
indicates that the Phase I window is representative of the rest of the clean
scene, not that the fit is optimal everywhere.

## Notes

* The limits assume that the residuals of the in-control image are close to
  standard normal. Always inspect the Phase I residual histogram and the
  output of `karma2d_diagnostics()` before trusting a limit.
* `limit` can also be a vector `c(lower, upper)` for asymmetric limits, and
  `morphology` can be `"closing"`, `"erosion"`, `"dilation"` or `"none"`.
* The residuals are computed from the neighbours actually observed in the
  scene, so an anomaly also perturbs the predictions of the pixels below and
  to the right of it.
